title: Light & Shadow
strapline: Torches, mirrors and a shadow that won't stay still — physics you can chase around the room.
intent: Children explore what light does — shines through, bounces off, gets blocked — and meet the words for it: transparent, opaque, reflection, shadow.
Children discover they can change a shadow on purpose: closer makes it bigger, further makes it smaller, move the torch and it swings.
Children make and test predictions with instant feedback — guess, shine, see.
Children explore how light tools work: switches, beams, mirrors, colour paddles, the overhead projector.
Children use light and shadow expressively — mixing colours on the lightbox, telling stories behind the shadow screen.
implementation: Build a den or blackout corner so children control the darkness — light play needs dark to push against.
Give children the torches. The learning is in their hands moving the beam, not in watching an adult demonstrate.
Offer a sorting basket of materials to test against the beam — cellophane, foil, card, net, bubble wrap — and wonder together which the light gets through.
Feed the vocabulary at the exact moment of discovery: 'it went straight through — it's transparent', 'your body blocked the light — that dark shape is your shadow'.
Ask for predictions before every test, and treat wrong guesses as the good bit: 'you thought it would shine through — what actually happened?'
On sunny days take it outside: chase shadows, draw round them in chalk, and come back after lunch to find they've sneaked off the lines.
Keep a shadow-puppet screen near the light source so exploration tips naturally into storytelling.
key_questions: What do you think the light will do when it hits this?
How could you make your shadow bigger without touching it?
Where has your shadow gone — and when will it come back?
What happens if we put the blue paddle on top of the yellow one?
Why do you think the shadow moved when you didn't?

impact.text: Children work the torches, switches and projector themselves, exploring how each one works.
Children test materials against the beam and sort them by what the light does — through, blocked, bounced.
Children predict what will happen before they shine the torch, then check — and revise when the light surprises them.
Children deliberately make shadows bigger and smaller and describe what they did — 'I moved the torch closer so it grew'.
Children ask real why-questions about light — 'why is my shadow long outside and little at lunch?' — and expect real answers.
Children layer colour paddles and cellophane on the lightbox to see what new colours they can make.
Children retell a favourite story behind the shadow screen with silhouette puppets.
Children use light words correctly in their talk — shadow, reflection, dark, shiny, see-through.

enhancements: A mirror box — three mirrors taped into a corner, one conker inside, suddenly six conkers.
Chalk shadow portraits in the garden at drop-off, revisited at pick-up: whose shadow moved and grew?
An overhead projector with translucent loose parts — glass beads, cellophane shapes, doilies — projected huge on the wall.
A shadow guessing game: familiar objects behind the screen, name them from silhouette alone.
Glow-in-the-dark stars and a 'charging station' — which light charges them best, and for how long do they glow?
Coloured cellophane on the windows for a week, washing the whole room blue then red.
A torch walk to the darkest corners of the setting, hunting for the shadows that live there.

playing_exploring: Darkness, torches and a den — the invitation is irresistible, and every beam swung is an experiment.
Children play with the same effect over and over, each repeat refining what they know.
active_learning: Instant feedback keeps children testing: shine, look, adjust, shine again.
They work at a shadow-shape or a colour mix until it does what they wanted.
creating_thinking: Predict-test-explain cycles are the beginnings of scientific thinking, run entirely by the child.
Children carry the ideas across contexts — spotting reflections in puddles and shadows at the lunch table.
